name: Expected loss (PD x LGD x EAD)
prompt: What is the dollar expected loss on a loan, built from the borrower's default risk and the facility's loss severity and exposure?

variables.meaning: expected loss, in dollars
probability of default (percentage/decimal), a property of the borrower
loss given default: percentage of the loan expected to be unrecoverable (= 100% minus recovery rate), a property of the facility
exposure at default: amount outstanding at the time of default, in dollars, a property of the facility

corruptions.why: The recovery rate is what you get back; the loss uses LGD = 1 - RR.
Without EAD this is a loss rate, not a dollar loss.
Higher loss severity must raise expected loss, so LGD multiplies rather than divides.

sensitivities.why: A borrower more likely to default raises the expected loss proportionally.
Less recovered after default means more lost.
More owed at default means more dollars at stake.

intuition: Will they default (borrower), how much is lost if they do and how much is owed (facility): multiply the three.

name: Capital adequacy ratio (CAR)
prompt: How is a bank's capital adequacy ratio defined, and what must it be at least?

variables.meaning: capital adequacy ratio; higher means a larger buffer to absorb losses
Tier 1 plus Tier 2 capital
RWA: assets weighted by riskiness (standardized weights or IRB)
regulatory minimum: 8% under Basel II, 10.5% under Basel III

corruptions.why: Capital is the buffer, so it goes on top; RWA is what it has to cover.
CAR uses risk-weighted assets, not unweighted total assets.
The regulator sets a floor, not a cap: CAR must be at least the minimum.

sensitivities.why: More Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital raises the buffer against the same risk.
Riskier assets need more capital, so the same capital covers a smaller share.

intuition: Capital over risk-adjusted assets: the buffer measured against how risky the balance sheet is, floored at 8% (Basel II) or 10.5% (Basel III).

name: Merton: equity payoff at T (long call on firm assets)
prompt: In the Merton model, what are shareholders worth at the debt's maturity, given the firm's asset value and the debt's face value?

variables.meaning: value of equity at T
value of the firm's assets at time T
principal amount due on the zero-coupon bond (face value of debt; the strike)

corruptions.why: That is a put payoff; equity is a call that pays when assets exceed the debt.
Without the floor at zero, equity could be negative; limited liability means shareholders just walk away.
min would make equity never positive; it is the max that caps the downside at zero.

sensitivities.why: Rises one-for-one with V_T when V_T exceeds F; flat at zero when V_T is below F.
Falls one-for-one with F while V_T exceeds F; no effect once equity is already worthless.

intuition: Equity is a call struck at the debt: shareholders keep everything above F and walk away with zero below it.

name: Merton: debt payoff at T (face less a short put)
prompt: In the Merton model, what do debtholders receive at maturity, written as the face value adjusted by an option payoff?

variables.meaning: value of debt at T
principal amount due on the zero-coupon bond (face value of debt; the strike)
value of the firm's assets at time T

corruptions.why: Debtholders are short the put: the shortfall is deducted from the face value, not added.
Subtracting a call would penalise debtholders when the firm does well; it is the put (shortfall) that is deducted.
That is only the put payoff; debt is the face value minus it.

sensitivities.why: Rises one-for-one with V_T while V_T is below F; capped at F once V_T exceeds F.
Rises with F while V_T exceeds F; once V_T is below F, debtholders get V_T regardless of F.

intuition: Debtholders are promised F but are short a put struck at F: below F they take the whole firm, above F they are capped at F.

name: Merton: equity value today as a BSM call on firm assets
prompt: Using Black-Scholes-Merton with no dividends, what is the firm's equity worth today in terms of asset value and debt?

variables.meaning: current value of the firm's equity
current value of the firm's assets
total debt to be repaid at time T (face value; the strike)
risk-free rate (decimal)
time to repayment in years
cumulative standard normal distribution function
BSM d_1 = [ln(V_0/D) + (r + sigma_V^2/2)T] / (sigma_V root T), with sigma_V the asset volatility
BSM d_2 = d_1 - sigma_V root T; equals the distance to default

corruptions.why: N(d_1) goes with the asset value and N(d_2) with the discounted strike, not the other way round.
Equity is a call: the discounted debt is paid out, so it is subtracted.
The debt is repaid at T, so it is discounted with e^{-rT}, not compounded.

sensitivities.why: A call is worth more when the underlying (firm assets) is worth more.
A higher strike (more debt ahead of equity) lowers the call value.
A higher rate lowers the present value of the debt to be repaid, raising the call value.

intuition: Equity is a call on the firm: asset value weighted by N(d_1) minus the present value of the debt weighted by N(d_2).

name: Merton: d1
prompt: In the Merton equity-as-a-call formula, how is d_1 computed from assets, debt, the risk-free rate, asset volatility and time?

variables.meaning: BSM d_1 for equity as a call on firm assets
current value of the firm's assets
total debt to be repaid at time T
risk-free rate (decimal)
asset volatility (decimal)
time to repayment in years

corruptions.why: With minus sigma-squared-over-two this is d_2 (the distance to default), not d_1.
The log ratio is assets over debt: more assets relative to debt must raise d_1.
Volatility scales with the square root of time, so the denominator is sigma times root T.

sensitivities.why: More assets relative to debt pushes the call deeper in the money.
More debt moves the strike up and the call out of the money.
A higher drift increases the numerator.

intuition: Log-moneyness of assets over debt plus drift (with +half variance), measured in units of asset volatility over the horizon.

name: Merton: d2 from d1
prompt: How is d_2 obtained from d_1 in the Merton/BSM equity formula?

variables.meaning: BSM d_2; equals the distance to default
BSM d_1
asset volatility (decimal)
time to repayment in years

corruptions.why: d_2 is always below d_1: one volatility-over-the-horizon is subtracted.
Volatility scales with root T, not T.
The Merton model is on firm assets, so asset volatility, not equity volatility, is used.

sensitivities.why: d_2 moves one-for-one with d_1.
A larger volatility gap is subtracted.
Holding d_1 fixed, a longer horizon subtracts more.

intuition: d_2 sits exactly one horizon-volatility below d_1.

name: Merton: distance to default (DtD = d2)
prompt: How many standard deviations are the firm's assets away from the face value of its debt in the Merton model?

variables.meaning: distance to default: number of standard deviations assets are from the default point; higher DtD means lower PD
BSM d_2
current value of the firm's assets
total debt to be repaid at time T (the default point)
risk-free rate (decimal)
asset volatility (decimal)
time to repayment in years

corruptions.why: Plus half the variance gives d_1; the distance to default is d_2, with minus.
Assets minus debt in logs: a firm with more assets must be further from default.
The standard deviation over the horizon is sigma times root T; dropping root T mis-scales the distance.

sensitivities.why: More assets relative to debt moves the firm further from default.
A higher default point brings the firm closer to it.
A higher drift raises expected terminal assets.
For a solvent firm (V_0 e^{rT} above D) higher volatility lowers DtD; for a deeply distressed firm it can raise it.

intuition: Log-distance from assets to the debt, plus drift, in units of asset volatility: more sigmas away means less likely to default.

name: Merton: risk-neutral probability of default
prompt: In the Merton model, what is the risk-neutral probability that the firm defaults, in terms of d_2?

variables.meaning: probability shareholders do not exercise their option to repay (assets grow at the risk-free rate)
cumulative standard normal distribution function
BSM d_2 = distance to default

corruptions.why: N(d_2) is the probability the call is exercised (no default); PD is its complement.
The exercise probability of the call uses d_2, not d_1.
A probability cannot exceed one; the complement is 1 minus N(d_2).

sensitivities.why: A larger distance to default means a lower probability of default.

intuition: Default is the call finishing out of the money: the left tail beyond minus the distance to default.

name: Merton: real-world probability of default
prompt: How does the Merton PD change when you use the firm's expected asset return instead of the risk-free rate?

variables.meaning: probability of default under real-world (physical) dynamics
cumulative standard normal distribution function
current market value of the firm's assets
face value of the debt (the default point)
expected return on the firm's assets (decimal)
asset volatility (decimal)
time horizon in years

corruptions.why: With r this is the risk-neutral PD; the real-world version swaps r for the expected asset return mu.
Without the leading minus this is the survival probability N(d_2), not the PD.
The drift term in d_2 carries minus half the variance.

sensitivities.why: More assets relative to the default point lowers the default probability.
A higher default point makes default more likely.
Faster expected asset growth moves the firm away from default.
Higher volatility raises PD for a firm whose expected assets exceed L (the usual case); it can lower it for a firm already expected to be below L.

intuition: Same N(-d_2), but the assets drift at the expected return mu instead of the risk-free rate.

name: CreditRisk+: Poisson probability of m defaults
prompt: In CreditRisk+, with n loans each with small default probability q, what is the probability of exactly m defaults in a year?

variables.meaning: probability of exactly m defaults over the year
(average) probability of default of each loan during the year (decimal, small)
number of loans (large)
number of defaults
expected number of defaults

corruptions.why: The Poisson weight is e to the minus the mean; e^{+qn} would give probabilities above one.
The factorial is of the number of defaults m, not the number of loans n.
Without dividing by m! the probabilities do not sum to one.

sensitivities.why: Raising q raises the probability of many defaults (m above qn) and lowers the probability of few defaults (m below qn).

intuition: Insurance maths for loans: Poisson with mean qn, the expected number of defaults.

name: RAROC (loan revenues over capital at risk)
prompt: How is the risk-adjusted return on capital of a loan defined?

variables.meaning: risk-adjusted return on capital; the loan is profitable if it exceeds the bank's cost of capital
after-tax income from the loan: loan value x (s + f - l - c)(1 - x)
capital needed to cover the risk: |Delta L| from duration, or the unexpected loan loss

corruptions.why: RAROC is a return: income on top, capital underneath.
Dividing by loan value gives a plain return on the loan; RAROC divides by the capital at risk.

sensitivities.why: More after-tax income on the same capital.
More capital tied up for the same income.

intuition: Return per dollar of risk capital: compare it with the bank's cost of capital to decide whether the loan pays.

name: RAROC numerator: after-tax loan revenues
prompt: What after-tax revenue does a loan generate from its spread, fees, expected losses, operating costs and tax rate?

variables.meaning: after-tax loan revenue, in dollars
value of the loan L, in dollars
spread between the loan rate and the bank's cost of capital (decimal)
fees attributable to the loan (decimal)
expected loan losses (decimal)
operating costs (decimal)
tax rate (decimal)

corruptions.why: Expected loan losses reduce revenue, so l is subtracted.
Tax takes a share away: the after-tax factor is 1 - x.
The (1 - x) tax factor multiplies the whole bracket; leaving it out gives pre-tax revenue.

sensitivities.why: A bigger loan earns the same margin on more dollars.
A wider spread is more income.
More fees add to income.
Higher expected losses eat into revenue.
Higher operating costs eat into revenue.
A higher tax rate leaves less after tax.

intuition: Spread plus fees, minus losses and costs, after tax, on the loan amount: add the two S/F earners, subtract the two L/C drains, then tax the lot.

name: RAROC denominator: capital at risk via duration (Delta L)
prompt: Using the loan's duration, how much could the loan's value change for an expected change in interest rates (the market-based capital at risk)?

variables.meaning: change in loan value; its magnitude is the capital at risk
loan value, in dollars
duration of the loan
expected change in interest rates (decimal)
current interest rate (decimal)

corruptions.why: The rate change is divided by 1 + i, not by i.
A rise in rates lowers the loan's value, so the change is negative.
Modified-duration scaling is Delta i over 1 + i.

sensitivities.why: On the sign of the rate change: for a rate rise (Delta i > 0) a larger loan makes Delta L more negative; for a rate fall it makes the gain larger.
On the sign of the rate change: for a rate rise longer duration means a bigger fall in value (Delta L more negative); for a rate fall a bigger gain.
The coefficient -L x D/(1+i) is negative, so a larger expected rate increase means a larger fall in the loan's value.
A higher current rate enlarges 1 + i and shrinks the size of Delta L toward zero: Delta L rises for a rate rise, falls for a rate fall.

intuition: Duration times the rate shock (scaled by 1 + i) times the loan: the value you could lose if rates rise.

name: RAROC alternative denominator: unexpected loan loss
prompt: Using historical default-rate data instead of market rates, what is the loan's capital at risk (unexpected loan loss)?

variables.meaning: capital at risk used in the RAROC denominator, in dollars
adjustment for unexpected default rates from the distribution of historical default rates (2.6 sigma at 99.5% if normal; higher, e.g. 5 or 6, for skewed loan distributions)
loss given default (decimal)
exposure at default, in dollars

corruptions.why: With PD this is the expected loss; the unexpected loss uses the tail adjustment alpha.
Losses scale with LGD, not the recovery rate.

sensitivities.why: A fatter tail of default rates needs more capital.
More lost per default means more capital at risk.
More exposure means more capital at risk.

intuition: Expected-loss shape, but with a tail multiplier alpha in place of PD: the loss in a bad year, not an average one.

name: Recovery rate from loss given default
prompt: How is the recovery rate on a defaulted loan obtained from its loss given default?

variables.meaning: recovery rate: percentage of the loan amount recovered after default
loss given default: percentage of the loan amount expected to be unrecoverable after default

corruptions.why: Recovery and loss split the loan amount between them, so LGD is subtracted from 100%.
100% minus PD is the survival probability; recovery is the complement of the loss severity LGD.

sensitivities.why: Every extra point lost after default is a point not recovered.

intuition: What you recover and what you lose after default add up to the whole loan.

name: Credit-adjusted value of derivatives (no-default value less CVA plus DVA)
prompt: What is the value of a derivatives portfolio once possible defaults of both the counterparty and the bank are taken into account?

variables.meaning: value of outstanding transactions allowing for possible defaults
no-default value (e.g. from Black-Scholes-Merton), assuming neither side defaults
credit valuation adjustment: PV of the expected cost to the bank of a counterparty default
debt valuation adjustment: PV of the expected cost to the counterparty of a bank default

corruptions.why: Both signs flipped: the counterparty's default risk costs the bank (minus CVA) and the bank's own default risk benefits it (plus DVA).
DVA is a cost to the counterparty, which increases the value to the bank, so it is added.
The bank's own default (DVA) also enters the credit-adjusted value.

sensitivities.why: A higher no-default value passes straight through.
More expected cost from the counterparty defaulting lowers the value.
The bank's own possible default is a benefit to the bank.

intuition: Start with the default-free price, pay for their default (minus CVA), get credit for your own (plus DVA).

name: CVA as a discounted sum over subintervals
prompt: How is CVA computed by splitting the life of the longest derivative into N subintervals?

variables.meaning: credit valuation adjustment
number of subintervals the life T of the longest outstanding derivative is divided into
probability of a counterparty default in subinterval i
present value of the loss from a counterparty default in subinterval i

corruptions.why: The starred quantities are for a bank default: that sum is DVA, not CVA.
The loss is weighted by the probability of default, not survival.
Summing probabilities alone gives a cumulative PD, not a dollar cost; each must be multiplied by the PV of the loss.

sensitivities.why: A more likely counterparty default in any subinterval raises CVA.
A larger PV of loss if the counterparty defaults raises CVA.

intuition: Probability they default in each slice times what you'd lose in that slice, added up.

name: DVA as a discounted sum over subintervals
prompt: How is DVA computed across the N subintervals, using the bank's own default probabilities?

variables.meaning: debt valuation adjustment
number of subintervals the life T of the longest outstanding derivative is divided into
probability of a bank default in subinterval i
present value of the resulting loss to the counterparty from a bank default in subinterval i

corruptions.why: Unstarred q_i and v_i refer to a counterparty default: that sum is CVA.
Mixes the bank's default probability with the loss from the counterparty's default.
Each PV of loss must be weighted by the probability of the bank defaulting in that subinterval.

sensitivities.why: A more likely bank default raises DVA (a benefit to the bank).
A larger PV of loss to the counterparty from a bank default raises DVA.

intuition: The mirror image of CVA: the same sum, starred, for your own default.

name: Hazard rate from the credit spread
prompt: How do you back out an average default intensity from a bond's credit spread and the recovery rate?

variables.meaning: average hazard rate (default intensity) per year up to T
credit spread for maturity T (decimal, per year)
recovery rate (decimal)

corruptions.why: The spread compensates for the loss, so divide by the loss rate 1 - RR, not the recovery rate.
Spread = hazard x loss rate, so the hazard is the spread divided by (1 - RR).
The loss rate is 1 minus the recovery rate.

sensitivities.why: A wider spread implies a higher default intensity.
If more is recovered, a given spread must be compensating for more frequent defaults.

intuition: Spread = default intensity x loss rate, so default intensity = spread / (1 - RR).

name: One-factor Gaussian copula: default probability conditional on the factor
prompt: In the one-factor Gaussian copula, what is the probability of default by T given a realization of the common factor?

variables.meaning: cumulative default probability by T conditional on the factor value F
unconditional cumulative default probability by time T
realization of the common factor (low F = bad state of the world)
copula correlation parameter
cumulative standard normal distribution function; N^{-1} its inverse

corruptions.why: F enters negatively: a low (bad) factor value must raise the conditional default probability.
The denominator is the idiosyncratic weight root(1 - rho), not root(rho).
The unconditional probability must first be mapped to a normal quantile with N^{-1}.

sensitivities.why: A higher unconditional PD raises the conditional PD in every state.
A better state of the world (higher F) lowers the conditional default probability.
On the factor F (and Q(T)): more correlation raises the conditional PD when F is low enough (a bad state) and lowers it when F is high (a good state).

intuition: Shift the PD's normal quantile down by root-rho times the factor, rescale by root(1 - rho): bad F, more defaults.

name: Worst case default rate (WCDR) at confidence X
prompt: What default rate will not be exceeded with confidence X under the one-factor Gaussian copula?

variables.meaning: worst case default rate at confidence level X
unconditional probability of default over the horizon
copula correlation parameter
confidence level (e.g. 0.999)
cumulative standard normal distribution function; N^{-1} its inverse

corruptions.why: In the WCDR form the percentile X enters positively (it is the conditional formula with F = -N^{-1}(X)).
The denominator is root(1 - rho).
PD must be converted to a normal quantile with N^{-1} before adding.

sensitivities.why: A higher average PD raises the worst case too.
A higher confidence level looks further into the bad tail.
At high confidence levels and small PDs (the usual case) more correlation raises WCDR; it can lower it otherwise.

intuition: Same as the conditional-PD formula with the worst factor F = -N^{-1}(X) plugged in: F enters negatively, X positively.

name: Credit VaR from the one-factor Gaussian copula
prompt: What is the credit VaR of a loan portfolio given its size, recovery rate and worst case default rate?

variables.meaning: credit VaR at the chosen confidence level
size of the loan portfolio
recovery rate (decimal)
worst case default rate at the chosen confidence level

corruptions.why: With the average PD this is the expected loss; VaR needs the worst case default rate.
The loss is the unrecovered share 1 - R, not the recovery rate.
Recoveries reduce the loss, so the factor is 1 - R.

sensitivities.why: A bigger portfolio has more at risk.
Higher recoveries mean smaller losses.
A higher worst case default rate means larger tail losses.

intuition: Expected-loss shape with the worst case default rate in place of PD: portfolio x loss rate x WCDR.

name: Basel III total Tier 1 capital (CET1 + AT1) minimum
prompt: Which two layers make up total Tier 1 capital under Basel III, and what minimum share of RWA must they reach?

variables.meaning: total Tier 1 capital
Common Equity Tier 1: common equity, retained earnings, unrealised gain/loss, minority interest (minimum 4.5% of RWA)
Additional Tier 1: non-cumulative perpetual preferred stock, CoCos, other minority interest (1.5% of RWA)
risk-weighted assets

corruptions.why: Tier 2 is a separate layer; Tier 1 plus Tier 2 is total capital.
8% is the total-capital minimum; total Tier 1 must be at least 6%.
4.5% is the CET1 minimum alone; with AT1's 1.5% total Tier 1 is 6%.

sensitivities.why: More common equity adds directly to Tier 1.
More additional Tier 1 instruments add to Tier 1.

intuition: 4.5 + 1.5 = 6: core equity plus additional Tier 1 makes total Tier 1.

name: Basel III total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) minimum
prompt: What makes up total capital under Basel III, and what minimum share of RWA must it reach (before buffers)?

variables.meaning: total regulatory capital
total Tier 1 capital (CET1 + AT1), at least 6% of RWA
subordinated debt over 5 years, preferred stock, general loan loss reserves (2% of RWA)
risk-weighted assets

corruptions.why: Basel III eliminated Tier 3 capital.
6% is the total Tier 1 minimum; total capital must be at least 8%.
The ratio is to risk-weighted assets; capital over total exposure is the separate 3% leverage ratio.

sensitivities.why: More Tier 1 capital adds to total capital.
More Tier 2 capital adds to total capital.

intuition: 6 + 2 = 8: Tier 1 plus Tier 2, at least 8% of RWA (10.5% once the conservation buffer is added in normal times).

name: Basel III leverage ratio
prompt: Which non-risk-weighted ratio of capital must a bank hold under Basel III, and what is the minimum?

variables.meaning: Basel III leverage ratio
capital
all balance sheet items plus off-balance-sheet items such as loan commitments (not risk-weighted)

corruptions.why: Dividing by RWA gives a capital adequacy ratio; the leverage ratio uses unweighted total exposure.
Capital is on top: the ratio is the capital cushion per dollar of exposure.
8% is the total-capital-to-RWA minimum; the leverage ratio minimum is 3%.

sensitivities.why: More capital raises the ratio.
More on- and off-balance-sheet exposure lowers the ratio.

intuition: A crude, un-risk-weighted backstop: capital over everything you are exposed to, at least 3%.

name: Liquidity coverage ratio (LCR)
prompt: Which ratio checks that a bank can survive 30 days of stressed cash outflows, and what is the minimum?
latex: \mathrm{LCR} = \frac{\text{high-quality liquid assets}}{\text{net cash outflows in a 30-day period}} \geq 100\%

variables.meaning: liquidity coverage ratio
HQLA after factors/haircuts (e.g. 100% for cash, central bank reserves, Treasuries; 0% for loans and fixed assets)
stressed outflows over 30 days: liability balances times run-off rates

decoys: \text{net cash outflows in a one-year period}

corruptions.latex: \mathrm{LCR} = \frac{\text{net cash outflows in a 30-day period}}{\text{high-quality liquid assets}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: Liquid assets must cover the outflows, so HQLA goes on top.

corruptions.latex: \mathrm{LCR} = \frac{\text{amount of available stable funding}}{\text{net cash outflows in a 30-day period}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: Available stable funding is the NSFR numerator; the LCR uses high-quality liquid assets.

corruptions.latex: \mathrm{LCR} = \frac{\text{high-quality liquid assets}}{\text{net cash outflows in a one-year period}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: The LCR horizon is 30 days of stress; one year is the NSFR horizon.

sensitivities.why: More liquid assets cover the same outflows more comfortably.
Larger stressed outflows need more cover.

intuition: Cash you can raise now over cash that could run in a month of stress: at least 100%.

name: Net stable funding ratio (NSFR)
prompt: Which ratio checks that a bank has enough stable funding over a one-year horizon, and what is the minimum?
latex: \mathrm{NSFR} = \frac{\text{amount of available stable funding}}{\text{amount of required stable funding}} \geq 100\%

variables.meaning: net stable funding ratio
ASF: liabilities and capital times ASF factors (e.g. 100% capital, 90% less stable retail deposits, 50% wholesale deposits)
RSF: assets times RSF factors (e.g. 0% cash, 65% mortgages, 85% short loans, 100% fixed assets)

corruptions.latex: \mathrm{NSFR} = \frac{\text{amount of required stable funding}}{\text{amount of available stable funding}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: Available funding must cover the requirement, so ASF goes on top.

corruptions.latex: \mathrm{NSFR} = \frac{\text{high-quality liquid assets}}{\text{amount of required stable funding}} \geq 100\%
corruptions.why: HQLA is the LCR numerator; the NSFR compares available with required stable funding.

corruptions.latex: \mathrm{NSFR} = \frac{\text{amount of available stable funding}}{\text{amount of required stable funding}} \geq 3\%
corruptions.why: 3% is the leverage-ratio minimum; the NSFR must be at least 100%.

sensitivities.why: More stable funding (capital, sticky deposits) raises the ratio.
More illiquid, long-term assets need more stable funding.

intuition: Stable money you have over stable money your assets need, over a year: at least 100%.

name: Trade compression: net notional exposure
prompt: After compressing offsetting positions on the same reference entity, maturity and coupon, what net notional remains?

variables.meaning: net notional of the single consolidated contract; its sign gives the net position (long if positive)
total notional of the long positions
total notional of the short positions

corruptions.why: Adding long and short gives the gross notional that compression reduces, not the net.
Long less short: a positive result is a net long held against the long-side counterparty.

sensitivities.why: More long notional increases the net long position.
More short notional offsets more of the longs.

intuition: Compression keeps the net and throws away the gross: longs minus shorts, one contract, same risk.
